### 论文描述（method.tex:49）

> **tail_decay**: proportion of tokens whose NLL exceeds the 90th percentile of the reference distribution (computed over C_0), measuring how heavy-tailed the NLL distribution is relative to human text.

### 代码实现（extract_features.py:79-141）

```python
# 1. 计算每个 token 位置的 log-softmax → (T-1, V)
log_probs = torch.log_softmax(token_logits, dim=-1)
# 2. 跨位置取均值，得到 vocabulary-level 的 avg log-prob → (V,)
avg_log_probs = log_probs.float().mean(dim=0)
# 3. 按 vocab 维度降序排列
sorted_lp, _ = torch.sort(avg_log_probs, descending=True)
# 4. 取 rank 100-1000 区间做线性回归
coeffs = np.polyfit(x, y, 1)
tail_decay = float(coeffs[0])  # 斜率
```

### 差异对比

| | 论文 | 代码 |
|---|---|---|
| 输入 | token-level NLL 序列 | vocabulary-level avg log-prob |
| 操作 | 超过 90th percentile 的 token 比例 | rank 100-1000 线性回归斜率 |
| 返回值 | proportion ∈ [0,1] | slope（负数） |
| 语义 | NLL 分布的尾部权重 | 词表概率分布的尾部衰减速率 |

> **tail_decay**: slope of the rank-ordered average log-probability distribution over the vocabulary. For each text, we compute the mean log-probability of each vocabulary token across all positions, sort these values in descending order, and fit a linear regression to ranks 100--1000. The slope measures how quickly the probability mass decays in the tail of the vocabulary distribution.

| 维度 | 论文 | 代码 |

| 操作 | 超过阈值的比例 | 线性回归斜率 |
| 返回值类型 | proportion ∈ [0,1] | slope（负数） |

> "tail_decay: slope of the vocabulary-level averaged log-probability distribution in the mid-rank region (ranks 100–1000), capturing how steeply the reference model's probability mass decays beyond the highest-probability tokens. A steeper (more negative) slope indicates a more concentrated distribution."

同时检查 sampling ablation 的 "85th-95th percentile" sensitivity analysis 描述是否需要对应修改。

Phenomenon characterization paper 的写作质量是核心竞争力。不能急着交卷。

**Why:** patch 堆叠出来的论文和从头精心构思的论文读起来不一样。审稿人 30 秒判断 abstract 价值，如果读起来像实验报告就已经失败。

**How to apply:**
- Abstract 必须有"故事感"：问题 → 洞察 → 方法 → 结果，每句推进叙事
- 每个 subsection 开头用问题或发现引导，不是"Table X reports Y"式的数据报告
- Discussion 要提供 insight，不是复述 Results
- Conclusion 不是 compressed abstract，要提炼"我们从递归生成中学到了什么"
- 删除 boilerplate（"remainder of this paper is organized as..."）
- 检查 patch 堆叠痕迹：段落是否像各自独立写的碎片而非连贯叙事

mean、TTR、hapax_ ratio）随深度单调漂移——文本越深，词汇多样性越低、entropy 越低，文本变得更\\\"平庸\\\" -  稳态特征 （entropy_ std、tail_ decay）几乎不随深度变化——NLL 分布的\\\"形状\\\"被采样机制和模型架构锁定 通俗讲：每次 LLM 续写都会让文本的\\\"平均水平\\\"往一个方向漂移（越来越可预测），但分布的\\\"波动形态\\\"不变。这就像河流的水位在涨，但波浪的形状没变。 Idea 利用这个 DDR 现象，我们可以做  ordinal depth estimation （序数深度估计）：不是判断\\\"人写还是AI写\\\"，而是判断\\\"这段文本经历了几轮 LLM 生成\\\"（gen-0 / gen-1 / Depth Discriminability ：7-feature ensemble 在 8 个 generator（3 个模型家族，0.6B-8.2B）上做 leave-one-generator-out 评估，3-class macro-F1 = 0.762，cross-model chains F1 = 0.809，显著优于所有单检测器 baseline (p <0.001) 2.  Differential Depth Response ：漂移特征和稳态特征互补——单独用任何一组都不如两组合起来。reference features 跨 generator 泛化更好，surface features 在域内更强，形成互补 3.  Negative Finding（诚实报告） ：depth-aware 数据筛选  不能  提升下游 CLM 训练质量。数据量是决定因素，不是深度组成。Depth fingerprinting 是诊断工具，不是治疗工具 Proposal / 我们提供的东西 1.  新任务定义 ：ordinal depth estimation——超越二分类，做生成深度的序数估计。这在文献中没有前人做过 2.  系统性实证验证 ：8 generators / 3 model families / 3 prompt types / 3 text domains，证明 DDR 是一个跨模型、跨域的稳健现象 3.  实用价值定位 ：depth fingerprinting 让数据清洗从"全删/全留"变成"按风险分层"——保留 gen-1（低风险），重点审查 gen-2+（高风险、分布漂移大） 4.  robustness 验证 ：随机词替换、LLM 语义改写、不同解码温度、跨域 seed 全部测试过 投稿目标：EMNLP 2026 ARR，DDL 5/25。论文已 submission-ready，正在做最终审查。

The paper explicitly acknowledges the architecture-dependent transfer gap (OLMo at 0.73 vs. Pythia-1B at 0.84), the ~ 3-class resolution ceiling, and positions the tool as \"diagnostic rather than curative.\" This calibrated framing is refreshing and mature. -  Interpretable mechanistic hypothesis.  The differential response pattern (location shift preserving functional form) is a testable, specific claim that goes beyond pure empiricism. The connection to attractor convergence theory for the 3-class ceiling is well-argued. -  End-to-end comparison adds depth.  The QLoRA experiment (Table 7) serves dual purpose: demonstrating richer depth signal exists beyond 7 features (CV F1=0.89) while exposing the generalization-robustness trade-off (17pp LOGO gap vs. XGBoost's 3pp gap). This strengthens the argument for interpretable features. 3. Weaknesses -  Severely limited generator scale.  All 5 generators are ≤2.8B parameters from only 3 families. The paper does not evaluate any model at 7B, 13B, or 70B+ scale. Larger, more capable generators produce more fluent text with potentially compressed depth margins — the already-visible degradation from Pythia-1B (0.84) to OLMo-2-1B (0.73) suggests performance could deteriorate significantly at larger scales. Without any evidence beyond 2.8B, generalizability claims are weak. -  Single reference model without sensitivity analysis.  All features are computed under a single held-out reference model (Pythia-410M). The paper provides no analysis of how results change with different reference models (e.g., a non-Pythia reference, or a larger reference model). This is a critical confound: features computed under a same-family reference (Pythia-410M evaluating Pythia-generated text) may behave differently than cross-family references. -  Feature set appears ad hoc despite principled framing.  The 7 features (5 NLL summary statistics + TTR + hapax_ ratio) are standard perplexity-based detection features repurposed for depth estimation. The retroactive \"differential response\" framing is neat but the feature selection itself is not derived from first principles. entropy_ min is acknowledged as \"borderline; architecture-dependent\" yet retained. No systematic feature search or information-theoretic justification is provided. -  Modest absolute performance and unclear per-document utility.  3-class LOGO F1=0.78 means substantial misclassification. Binary F1=0.71 implies ~ 29% error. The paper positions depth profiling as a corpus-level diagnostic tool, but provides no experimental validation of corpus-level composition estimation accuracy (e.g., estimating the gen-2+ fraction in a mixed corpus at various sizes). -  Downstream experiment insufficiently described.  The negative downstream result — depth-aware curation doesn't beat random subsampling — is a significant finding but receives only brief treatment. No dedicated section, no table showing the comparison, and no details on the experimental setup (corpus size, model trained, evaluation metrics, number of seeds, confidence intervals). This undermines one of the paper's claimed contributions. -  Single domain.  All generation chains use English Wikipedia seeds. No evaluation on other domains (creative writing, code, scientific text, social media, multilingual). TTR and hapax_ ratio are highly domain-sensitive; the differential response pattern may not hold across domains. -  Paraphrastic comparison lacks depth.  Table 5 shows the comparison but the analysis is brief (~ 1 paragraph). Cross-transfer results (0.65–0.68 F1) are interesting but not discussed in terms of practical implications. The connection to attractor convergence theory predictions deserves more than a passing mention. -  Sparse related work.  Only 10 references. Missing citations to important works: FineWeb/CCNet perplexity filtering at scale, Alemohammad et al. (2024) on self-consuming generative models (cited but could be discussed more), recent multi-class source attribution work (SemEval-2024 Task 8), and deeper engagement with the model collapse theoretical literature. 4. Summary This paper introduces ordinal depth estimation as a new task: given a text, predict how many recursive LLM generation steps it has undergone (generation depth 0–4). The authors characterize \"differential depth response\" — central-tendency/diversity features (entropy mean, TTR, hapax ratio) drift monotonically with depth while distributional shape features (entropy std, tail decay) remain stationary. A 7-feature XGBoost ensemble achieves 0.83 macro-F1 within-generator and 0.81 under leave-one-generator-out (LOGO) cross-validation across 5 generators from 3 model families. Additional experiments cover paraphrastic vs. continuation chains, finer-grained 5-class ordinal classification (F1=0.51, concordance=0.82), and end-to-end QLoRA classifiers that achieve higher within-generator accuracy (0.91) but degrade under LOGO (0.72), validating the robustness advantage of interpretable features. 2. Strengths -  Genuinely novel task formulation.  No prior work attempts ordinal depth estimation. The move beyond binary real/synthetic detection is well-motivated by the reality of recursive generation chains in web-scale corpora. The framing as an ordinal classification problem with formal LOGO evaluation protocol is a meaningful contribution to the research agenda (§1, §3.1). -  Clean empirical characterization.  The differential depth response — drift vs. stationary feature partition — is demonstrated convincingly. Table 2 shows a sharp bifurcation: drift features have R² > 0.88 while stationary features have R²  < 0.20. The location-shift interpretation is mechanistically coherent and well-supported by the perplexity validation (13.5 → 1.72 across depths, Spearman ρ = −0.92). -  Strong cross-generator generalization.  LOGO macro-F1 = 0.81 with per-generator std = 0.032 across 5 generators from 3 distinct families (Tables 3–4) is a strong result. The leave-one-family-out evaluation showing only −1.5pp additional degradation beyond generator-level holdout is particularly convincing for architecture-invariance claims. -  Comprehensive experimental coverage.  The paper covers five distinct experimental dimensions: feature ablation (§4.1), cross-generator evaluation (§4.2), chain-type comparison (§4.3), granularity analysis (§4.4), and end-to-end neural classifiers (§4.5). Each addresses a natural question about the phenomenon. -  Informative negative/bounded results.  The 5-class result (F1=0.51, concordance=0.82) is honestly reported as establishing a practical ceiling. The gen-2/gen-3 confusion (42%) is well-explained by diminishing drift returns. The E2E generalization gap (−19pp under LOGO) provides genuine insight about the interpretability–robustness tradeoff. -  Well-designed evaluation protocol.  LOGO is the right evaluation for generalization claims. Feature ablation confirms complementarity rather than redundancy. The paraphrastic comparison provides theoretical validation via attractor convergence predictions. -  Clear writing.  The paper is well-organized, with clean logical flow from motivation through characterization to practical implications. Each experiment section states the question, presents results, and interprets findings concisely. 3. Weaknesses -  (Major) Limited model scale.  All 5 generators are ≤2.8B parameters, and all are base (pretrained) models. Real-world recursive generation chains are more likely to involve instruction-tuned models at larger scales (7B–70B+). The model collapse literature suggests that distributional drift attenuates with model capacity. Without testing on larger or instruction-tuned models, the practical applicability of the findings to realistic contamination scenarios is uncertain. The paper acknowledges this in Limitations (§6), but this is a fundamental gap between the motivating scenario and experimental scope. -  (Major) Synthetic chain construction.  All chains use single-model continuation where the same generator produces all depths. Real-world contamination involves heterogeneous generators, diverse prompts, varying decoding parameters, and human editing at each step. The paper tests only a single continuation prompt and fixed sampling parameters (though these details are not fully specified in the method section). The practical relevance of the controlled experimental setup to the motivating real-world problem is unclear. -  (Major) Limited methodological novelty.  The features (NLL entropy statistics, TTR, hapax ratio) are entirely standard stylometric and detection features. The classifier (XGBoost) is off-the-shelf. The observation that recursive generation reduces lexical diversity and increases predictability is well-established in the model collapse literature (Shumailov et al., 2024). The paper's contribution is primarily in (a) formulating the ordinal task and (b) empirically characterizing the drift/stationary partition — the methodology itself is not novel. -  (Minor) Reference model dependency underexplored.  All experiments use Pythia-410M as the reference model. The paper lists this as a limitation but does not ablate reference model choice. Given that Pythia-410M shares architecture with two of the five generators (Pythia-1B, Pythia-2.8B), within-family feature extraction could inflate performance for Pythia generators. The higher F1 for Pythia-1B (0.86, highest in Table 3) is consistent with this concern. -  (Minor) Narrow domain and language.  Seed texts presumably come from a single domain (not specified in the paper). No cross-domain or cross-language experiments are reported. Depth drift dynamics could vary substantially across registers (news, social media, creative writing, code). -  (Minor) Feature ablation labeling is confusing.  In Table 1, \"Surface only (2 features)\" refers to TTR and hapax_ ratio, while \"Reference only (5 features)\" refers to the 5 entropy-based features requiring the reference model. But Section 3.3 categorizes features into \"Drifting\" (4 features including TTR and hapax) and \"Stationary\" (3 features). These are two different partitions that are not clearly distinguished, potentially confusing readers about what \"surface\" vs \"reference\" means relative to \"drifting\" vs \"stationary.\" -  (Minor) Some references appear placeholder.  \"Brokentel et al., 2025\" and \"Attractor Authors, 2025\" in the Related Work section look like anonymized placeholder citations. If these are real papers, the citation format should match standard conventions; if they are the authors' own work, this compromises anonymity. -  (Minor) Missing figures.  The paper contains 10 tables but no figures in the main text. A visualization of the differential depth response (feature values × depth, as described in the experiment design) would greatly strengthen the core empirical contribution. The strip plot / feature trend visualization seems planned but absent from the submitted PDF. 4. Questions for Authors 1.  Reference model ablation:  How sensitive are results to reference model choice? But the most parsimonious explanation is  reference-model mismatch : Pythia-410M naturally produces more informative entropy statistics for same-family generators. All 5 generators are base (non-instruction-tuned) models. Since virtually all deployed LLMs are instruction-tuned and RLHF-aligned, the practical relevance for real-world depth estimation is unclear. The paper does not test or discuss instruction-tuned models at all. If depth signal collapses even more under RLHF (plausible given modified sampling distributions), the already-weak results would become entirely impractical. The paper establishes where depth estimation works and fails but does not demonstrate any downstream application. The "second-order fingerprint" claim lacks validation. Corpus-level depth composition estimation (a natural application) is not tested. With only depths 0–4, the paper cannot characterize long-run convergence behavior. The attractor convergence finding for paraphrastic chains (convergence by gen-3) would benefit from deeper chains to confirm the plateau. 4. Questions for Authors 1. Scale confound.  Pythia-2.8B is both the largest generator and shows the strongest depth signal. Could the architecture-conditional pattern partly reflect scale differences? Can you provide even a simple experiment demonstrating that depth-response profiles actually discriminate generator families? E.g., clustering generators by their 7-dimensional slope vectors and showing family separation? 5.  Tokenizer confound.  You note that Qwen uses a different tokenizer (byte-level BPE vs GPT-NeoX). Could the weak surface feature correlations for Qwen partly reflect tokenizer mismatch in TTR/hapax computation? If TTR is computed at the token level, different tokenizers produce incomparable values. 5. All generators are ≤2.8B, and the visible degradation trend (0.84 → 0.73 across architectures) raises serious concerns about applicability to the 7B–70B+ models that dominate real-world LLM text generation. Without any evidence at larger scale, the findings may reflect properties of small models rather than universal depth signals. 2.  Single reference model is a critical uncontrolled variable.  Features computed under Pythia-410M scoring Pythia-generated text (same family) may yield artificially clean signals. No sensitivity analysis to reference model choice is provided. 3.  Practical impact is unclear.  The paper's own negative downstream result eliminates the primary applied motivation (data curation). The corpus-level diagnostic use case is asserted but not empirically validated. This leaves the contribution as primarily an empirical characterization study, which needs stronger evidence of generality to justify venue-level impact. 4.  Missing methodological details.  The downstream experiment — one of three claimed contributions — lacks sufficient detail for reproducibility. The paper would benefit from: (a) evaluation with at least one 7B+ generator, (b) reference model sensitivity analysis, (c) a proper downstream experiment section with full methodology, and (d) corpus-level estimation validation. Addressing (a) and (b) would substantially strengthen the contribution claim.

% Abstract — Depth Fingerprinting of Recursive LLM Generation Chains
\begin{abstract}
When LLM-generated text re-enters the web and seeds further generation, the resulting recursive chains exhibit progressively altered distributional properties, complicating provenance tracking and quality-aware data curation.
We ask whether this drift is structured enough to estimate how many generation steps a text has undergone, framing this as \emph{ordinal depth estimation} (classifying text as gen-0\,/\,gen-1\,/\,gen-2+ rather than binary real-vs-synthetic).
Studying eight base models from five families, we identify a \emph{differential depth response}: central-tendency features (mean entropy, lexical diversity) drift monotonically with generation depth, while shape features (entropy max, vocabulary tail slope) remain near-stationary.
This pattern is consistent with a location shift in the token-level NLL distribution that preserves distributional shape.

We further show that this structured drift does not translate into training utility: depth-aware data curation offers no improvement over random subsampling at equal sample count.
\end{abstract}

\section{Method}
\label{sec:method}

\subsection{Task Formulation}
\label{sec:task}

Given a text $x$, the goal is to predict its \emph{generation depth} $d \in \{0, 1, 2{+}\}$, where $d{=}0$ denotes human-written text, $d{=}1$ denotes first-generation LLM output conditioned on human text, and $d{=}2{+}$ denotes text produced by recursively conditioning an LLM on its own prior output at least twice.
Formally, let $\mathcal{C}_0$ be a reference corpus of human-written text.
A generation chain of depth $k$ is defined recursively: $x^{(0)} \sim \mathcal{C}_0$, and $x^{(k)} = G(x^{(k-1)})$ for $k \geq 1$, where $G$ denotes stochastic LLM generation conditioned on its input.
We frame depth estimation as an ordinal classification task over three classes rather than binary real-vs-synthetic detection, enabling finer-grained provenance characterization.
Depths beyond 2 are merged into a single $2{+}$ class, consistent with monotonic feature convergence that compresses inter-class margins beyond depth 2 (\S\ref{sec:results-differential}).

\subsection{Generation Chain Construction}
\label{sec:generation}

We construct generation chains using eight generators spanning five model families: \textbf{Pythia} (2.8B, 1B) \cite{pythia}, \textbf{OLMo} (OLMo-2-1B) \cite{olmo}, \textbf{Qwen} (Qwen3-1.7B, Qwen3-0.6B, Qwen3-8B-Base) \cite{qwen3}, \textbf{Llama} (Llama-3.2-3B) \cite{llama3}, and \textbf{Mistral} (Mistral-7B-v0.3) \cite{mistral7b}.
This selection covers parameter scales from 0.6B to 8B and diverse pretraining corpora, enabling evaluation of cross-generator and cross-scale generalization.

For each generator, we sample approximately 1{,}000 seed passages from English Wikipedia as $\mathcal{C}_0$.
The same pool of seed passages serves as gen-0 for all generators.
We use shared seeds across generators to ensure that cross-generator comparisons control for input content, isolating the effect of the generation model from source text variation.
In LOGO evaluation, gen-0 samples from the held-out generator's chains also appear (with the same text) in the training generators' chains, creating a potential train--test overlap for the gen-0 class.
We address this with a supplementary binary evaluation excluding gen-0 entirely (\S\ref{sec:results-baselines}).
Each seed is iteratively fed through the generator to produce a chain of depth 4 (i.e., gen-0 through gen-4), using the prompt ``\texttt{Continue the following text: \{text\}}''.
All generation uses temperature $\tau{=}0.7$, nucleus sampling with $p{=}0.9$, and maximum length of 256 new tokens.
The theoretical yield is $8 \times {\sim}1{,}000 \times 5 \approx 40{,}000$ texts; after removing generation failures, exact duplicates, and passages shorter than 50 tokens, 37{,}058 texts remain (Appendix~\ref{app:dataset-stats}).
For classification, depths 2--4 are collapsed into the $2{+}$ class.

\label{sec:features}

The seven features are motivated by two complementary views of distributional drift.
Reference-model features capture how the text's token-level surprise distribution shifts relative to a fixed model; surface features capture how lexical diversity contracts under recursive generation.
Together, they span both the generative mechanism (what the model produces) and the surface manifestation (how the vocabulary changes).
This two-pronged design is not post-hoc: it follows directly from the hypothesis that recursive generation induces a location shift in the NLL distribution (\S\ref{sec:results-differential}).

We extract seven distributional features per text, organized into two groups based on what they measure rather than how they are computed.

\paragraph{Reference-model features.}
A held-out reference model (Pythia-410M, chosen to be smaller than all generators) computes per-token negative log-likelihood (NLL) for each text.

1	\section{Discussion}
2	\label{sec:discussion}
3	
4	\paragraph{Why does shape remain stationary?}
5	The softmax architecture and sampling hyperparameters that determine distributional shape are fixed across depths.
6	Recursive generation shifts context toward high-probability regions, reducing entropy mean, but does not alter the generation mechanism itself.
7	This account predicts stationarity until the model reaches its fixed-point distribution, a regime not observed at chain length $\leq$4.
8	Sampling ablation provides a natural test: depth signal is robust when sampling noise is low ($t \in [0.5, 0.7]$, ${\leq}0.3$\,pp degradation) but degrades at $t = 1.0$ ($-6$\,pp; Appendix~\ref{app:sampling-sensitivity}), where sampling randomness overwhelms the systematic location shift.
9	
10	\paragraph{Prompt-type dependence.}
11	Continuation chains yield the strongest signal (F1\,=\,0.781 vs.\ 0.730 for elaboration), with cross-type transfer at 0.753 (Appendix~\ref{app:prompt-type}).
12	Semantic-preservation constraints attenuate drift, consistent with \citet{broken_telephone}: the more a task anchors the output distribution to the input, the less room recursive drift has to accumulate.
13	
14	\paragraph{Practical applicability.}
15	At the document level, gen-1 per-class F1\,=\,0.63 (37\% misclassification) is insufficient for automated filtering but sufficient for corpus-level flagging, where error scales as $O(1/\sqrt{n})$ and aggregate depth composition estimates become reliable.
16	Error analysis (Appendix~\ref{app:error-analysis}) confirms that misclassifications concentrate in shallow gen-2+ samples where drift has not yet accumulated, consistent with DDR predictions.
17	
18	\paragraph{Relation to model collapse.}
19	Model collapse \cite{curse_of_recursion,strong_model_collapse} describes degradation when models are \emph{retrained} on their own outputs.
20	Our inference-chain drift occurs without parameter updates, potentially representing an early, reversible stage of the same distributional narrowing.
21	Topic drift accounts for $<$9\% of feature variance ($R^2 = 0.082$), confirming it mediates rather than confounds depth signal.
22	
23	\paragraph{Granularity and robustness.}
24	Three classes represent the practical resolution ceiling: 5-class LOGO F1 drops to $\approx$0.50, with depths 2--4 mutually indistinguishable (Appendix~\ref{app:finer-depth}).
25	That said, QLoRA fine-tuning recovers 3-class F1\,=\,0.905 (Appendix~\ref{app:qlora}), confirming that richer signal exists beyond the seven summary statistics.
26	Under text perturbation, LLM-simulated sentence regeneration (50\% edit distance) causes comparable degradation to 5\% random word replacement (Appendix~\ref{app:human-edit}), confirming that depth signal resides in generative structure rather than surface token statistics.
27	
28	\paragraph{Instruction tuning.}
29	Instruction-tuned models show substantially weaker fingerprints (OLMo-Instruct LOGO F1\,=\,0.338 vs.\ 0.764 base).
30	Length regulation and format constraints imposed by alignment compress the distributional variation that depth fingerprinting exploits, justifying our restriction to base models as the appropriate setting for isolating the phenomenon.
31

1	\section{Conclusion}
2	\label{sec:conclusion}
3	
4	We introduced ordinal generation depth estimation and documented a differential depth response across eight base-model generators from five families: recursive generation induces a systematic location shift in the token-level NLL distribution while preserving distributional shape, and this structured drift is detectable with a lightweight 7-feature ensemble (3-class F1\,=\,0.809 on cross-model chains, 0.762 under LOGO).
5	The finding that depth-aware data curation provides no downstream benefit despite structured distributional change suggests that the drift captured by depth fingerprinting is orthogonal to the text properties that determine training utility.
6	
7	Two boundaries define the scope of these results.
8	First, instruction tuning compresses the distributional variation that fingerprinting exploits; extending to aligned models requires disentangling format-induced and depth-induced drift.
9	Second, while the signal generalizes across generators up to 8B parameters, frontier-scale models (70B+) with higher fluency may further compress feature margins.
10	All code, data, and trained models will be released upon publication.

\section{Conclusion}
\label{sec:conclusion}

We introduced ordinal generation depth estimation and documented a differential depth response across eight base-model generators from five families: recursive generation induces a systematic location shift in the token-level NLL distribution while preserving distributional shape, and this structured drift is detectable with a lightweight 7-feature ensemble (3-class F1\,=\,0.809 on cross-model chains, 0.762 under LOGO).
The finding that depth-aware data curation provides no downstream benefit despite structured distributional change suggests that the drift captured by depth fingerprinting is orthogonal to the text properties that determine training utility.

Two boundaries define the scope of these results.
First, instruction tuning compresses the distributional variation that fingerprinting exploits; extending to aligned models requires disentangling format-induced and depth-induced drift.
Second, while the signal generalizes across generators up to 8B parameters, frontier-scale models (70B+) with higher fluency may further compress feature margins.
All code, data, and trained models will be released upon publication.
